Though it remains scientifically dubious, I've always been intrigued by the Aquatic Ape Theory which suggests that human hair traits relate to a semi-aquatic phase of human development. As the idea goes, some subspecies of human had adapted to living a life at shore, relying on the sea for food and a way to escape land predators. And so they evolved traits suited to spending a lot of time in the water much like otters or seals. Reduced body hair streamlined the body for faster swimming while long head hair, particularly with females, provided a means for infants to stay with their parents in the water by clinging to their hair. Male pattern baldness was explained as a trait to further streamline the males to facilitate their hunting activity in the water. The idea never amounted to anything, but it offers an entertaining vision of early life very different from the usual caveman notions.

And then there are the Boskops or Boskop Hominids. This was a suspected subspecies of human whose remains were discovered in Boskop South Africa in a region that, when they were supposedly alive, was believed to be near shore. Though not taken very seriously today, when they were found in the early 20th century a theory developed that these people had a 30% larger cranial capacity than contemporary humans along with diminutive stature and child-like facial features. It was suggested that they lived primarily on shellfish and enjoyed a peaceful carefree existence living on the bounty of the shore. There has long been wild speculation as to what these people might have actually used that extra 30% of brain size for. No longer regarded as a subspecies, scientists today suggest the difference in cranial volume was a misinterpretation. But I still like to imagine the lifestyle of the Great Gazoo Tribe.
